summary:
**Conversation Overview**

Bethany, co-founder and CEO of The Luxora Collective (a revenue growth partner for independent med spa owners), asked Claude to build a complete one-hour lead-magnet webinar system for med spa owners doing $500K to $2M annually. The deliverable needed to incorporate material from a colleague named Ashley, TLC's existing playbooks and client-facing resources, and be promoted via Meta ads, with a pitch at the end designed to convert attendees into clients.

Claude produced a comprehensive system including positioning strategy, five Meta ad variations with full copy, a registration page, a show-up sequence, a minute-by-minute run of show, word-for-word scripts for every segment, the full offer pitch, Q&A close with seeded objection handling, a 14-day post-event email cadence, and a pre-flight checklist. The initial build was structured around a "course fatigue" positioning angle. Bethany corrected this direction, clarifying that most med spa owners at this level have never bought a course and do not identify with that pain, making the angle ineffective.

Bethany provided a detailed brief on the actual emotional pain points the audience lives with daily: financial anxiety around revenue that disappears before reaching the owner, feeling trapped in a business that owns them, inability to trust their team to sell, frustration with agency spending that produces ghosting and low-quality inquiries, patient retention failures, staffing instability, decision fatigue, comparison to competitors appearing to succeed on social media, and deep fear of failure after significant personal investment. She clarified that what these owners actually want is predictable revenue, a team they can trust, patients who return, and a business that does not depend on their constant presence, and that messaging must sell freedom, predictability, and confidence rather than marketing tactics or appointment volume.

Claude rebuilt the entire system from scratch around this emotional framework. The new positioning spine is "revenue that requires you isn't an asset, it's a job with extra risk," demonstrated through a contrast between two practices at identical revenue with completely different structures and lives. The nine pain points were clustered into three teaching blocks: the money (financial fear, agency frustration, decision fatigue resolved through margin math and real acquisition cost), the team (distrust and staffing addressed structurally through the three teachable differences and compensation design), and the return (retention and recurring revenue as the path to predictability and freedom). Fear of failure is named once in the origin story for permission-giving purposes and never exploited. All five ads, all scripts, and the post-event cadence were rewritten to lead with emotional outcome and prove it with mechanism. A colleague named Aanchal is referenced as a potential chat moderator for the live event. The dual CTA structure was retained: a partnership application as the primary close and a $29 Revenue Leak Audit as the secondary, reframed as "stop guessing about your own business" rather than a downsell.

# The Luxora Collective
## The 60-Minute Masterclass System
### Ad campaign, run of show, word-for-word scripts, pitch, and follow-up cadence

---

# PART 1: THE STRATEGIC FRAME

## 1.1 The working title

**Primary title:**
> **The 50-Client Blueprint: How Med Spas Doing $500K to $2M Add 50 Paying Clients in 90 Days Without Buying Another Course**

**Alternates to split-test in ad creative:**
- The Revenue Leak Masterclass: Why Your Med Spa Doesn't Have a Lead Problem
- The $200,000 You Already Earned and Never Collected
- Course Fatigue: What to Do After the Fifth Program Didn't Work

The title carries the course-fatigue angle, which is already the primary positioning for paid traffic. It does double duty here: it names the pain and it pre-frames why a done-with-you partnership is different from the programs they already bought.

## 1.2 Who this is built for

Independent med spa owners doing $500K to $2M annually. Typically owner-operated, often an injector or an RN who built a book of business and then hit a ceiling. They have bought at least one program, course, or coaching container that did not stick. They are busy in the treatment room, not the CEO seat.

## 1.3 The single big idea

**You do not have a lead problem. You have a leak problem. And no course will ever fix a leak, because information does not install.**

Every teaching segment, every ad, every email, and the pitch itself ladder up to that one sentence. If an attendee remembers nothing else, they should remember that.

## 1.4 The conversion architecture (decide this before you build the page)

You have two viable paths. I recommend Path A.

**Path A: Dual-CTA (recommended)**
- Primary close on the call: apply for a Growth Partnership Blueprint Call. Limited seats, application-gated.
- Secondary close for everyone who is not ready: the $29 Revenue Leak Audit with KPI Calculator.

This is the strongest structure for a $9,000 to $15,000 offer, because the $29 audit converts the 80 percent who will never book a call from a cold webinar, and the audit itself is the natural on-ramp to the Blueprint Call two weeks later. Nobody leaves empty-handed, and nobody leaves un-monetized.

**Path B: Single-CTA to application only**
Cleaner and higher perceived value, but you leave the majority of the room unconverted and you rebuild the same audience from scratch next month.

**Recommendation: run Path A.** Pitch the partnership first at full conviction, then present the $29 audit as the "start smaller" door rather than as a discount. Never let the audit read as a consolation prize. Frame it as step one of the same methodology.

## 1.5 Benchmarks to hold yourself to

| Metric | Acceptable | Good | Excellent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ad click-through rate | 1.0% | 1.8% | 2.5%+ |
| Registration page conversion | 25% | 35% | 45%+ |
| Cost per registration | $18 | $12 | $8 |
| Show-up rate (live) | 25% | 35% | 45%+ |
| Stay-to-pitch rate | 50% | 65% | 75%+ |
| $29 audit take rate (of attendees) | 8% | 15% | 22%+ |
| Applications booked (of attendees) | 3% | 6% | 10%+ |
| Application to closed partnership | 15% | 25% | 35%+ |

Run the math on your own numbers before you spend a dollar. At 200 registrations, a 35 percent show rate, and a 6 percent application rate, you are booking roughly 4 calls per webinar. At a 25 percent close on a $9,000 partnership, that is one client per event, plus the audit revenue and the follow-up conversions. That is a profitable machine only if you run it weekly, so build it to be repeatable, not perfect.

---

# PART 2: THE META AD CAMPAIGN

## 2.1 Campaign structure

- **Objective:** Leads (on-site conversion, Lead event fired on registration confirmation)
- **Budget:** Start at $60 to $100 per day for 7 days before judging anything
- **Campaign:** One campaign, Advantage+ audience with a lookalike or interest seed
- **Ad sets:**
  1. Broad, age 30 to 60, women 75 percent weighted, US, Advantage+ placements
  2. Interest stack: Botox, dermal filler, medical spa, Allergan, Galderma, aesthetic practice, med spa owner, American Med Spa Association

If your consult close rate is costing you eighty-five thousand a year, and it is for most practices this size, the partnership pays for itself before we finish the install. The expensive option is the one where nothing changes for another year.

**"What if it doesn't work for me?"**
> That's what the Premium tier's guarantee is for, in writing. And it's what the Blueprint Call is for. If I don't think we can produce a return for you, I'll tell you on that call and I won't take your money. I'd rather have a clean no than a bad client.

## The final close

> We're at time. Two links, one last time.
>
> If you know, apply for the Blueprint Call. Three spots.
>
> If you're not there yet, take the twenty-nine dollar Revenue Leak Audit. Everyone should do that one.
>
> And if you do neither, please do this: run the five leaks on your own practice this week. Write the dollar number next to each one. That exercise alone is worth the hour you gave me, and you deserve to know what those numbers are.
>
> Thank you for your time. It's the most expensive thing you own and you spent an hour of it with me. I don't take that lightly. Go find your money.

---

# PART 7: POST-EVENT EMAIL CADENCE

Built on Ashley's post-event cadence structure, adapted for this webinar. Segment on day two by behavior: attendees who bought the audit, attendees who did not, and no-shows.

| Day | Segment | Subject | Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0, within 2 hours | All attendees | The links from today's class | Replay for 48 hours, both CTAs, one-paragraph recap of the five leaks. Short. |
| 0 | No-shows | You missed it, here's one thing | Deliver the single highest-value leak in full. Replay access for 24 hours only. Both links. |
| 1 | Non-buyers | The leak nobody wants to talk about | Full teardown of the consult close rate leak with the math. Ends on the $29 audit. |
| 2 | Non-buyers | What Monday looks like | The implementation gap. Course fatigue story. Ends on the Blueprint Call application. |
| 3 | Non-buyers | 50 clients in 90 days, in writing | The guarantee explained in detail, including the contingencies, because transparency about the contingencies increases belief rather than reducing it. |
| 4 | Non-buyers | Objection email | The three reasons owners say no, answered directly. Price, timing, team buy-in. |
| 5 | Non-buyers | Replay is coming down | Final urgency. Both links. Spots remaining. |
| 7 | Audit buyers | Your audit, and what to do with it | Delivery plus the natural upgrade path to the Blueprint Call. This is your highest-converting segment. Give it the most attention. |
| 10 | All non-buyers | The one calculation | Pure value. Capacity ceiling walkthrough. Rebuilds goodwill and re-engages openers for the next event. |
| 14 | All non-buyers | Invitation to the next class | Roll them into the next webinar cohort. Never let a registrant list go cold. |

Two rules for this sequence. First, every email delivers something usable even if the reader never buys, because your list is a long-term asset and burning it for one launch is expensive. Second, the audit-buyer segment is your warmest revenue: those people paid you money and self-identified. Call them, do not just email them.

---

# PART 8: TECH, TEAM, AND CHECKLIST

## Stack
- **Platform:** Zoom Webinar or StreamYard into a custom page. Avoid platforms that make attendees install anything.
- **Registration and follow-up:** GHL, with the revenue-range field mapped to a segmentation tag from the start.
- **Slides:** Roughly 30 to 40. Mostly one number or one sentence per slide. No paragraphs. The leak math slides should build one line at a time.
- **Chat moderator:** Aanchal or a team member, in the chat the whole time, dropping links on cue, answering logistics, flagging good questions and buying signals for you. This role is worth real money and is routinely skipped.

## Pre-flight checklist
1. Run the full script out loud with a timer, twice. Adjust to fit 60 minutes with 5 minutes of slack.
2. Pull three real client leak examples with actual dollar figures to use in Block 1. Anonymized. Specificity is the whole game.
3. Have both links pre-written in a text file so the moderator can paste instantly.
4. Confirm the application form and the $29 checkout both work on mobile. Test them on your own phone.
5. Decide the real number of partnership spots before you go live and never say a number you will not honor.
6. Set the replay window and enforce it.
7. Record everything. The first three runs are rehearsal for the evergreen version.

## After three live runs
Take the highest-converting recording, cut it into an evergreen replay funnel, and run cold traffic to it continuously. Keep one live event monthly for fresh material and testimonials. The live version is where the offer gets sharpened. The evergreen version is where it scales.

### Ad campaign, run of show, word-for-word scripts, pitch, and follow-up cadence

# PART 1: THE STRATEGIC FRAME

## 1.1 The working title

**Primary title:**
> **The 50-Client Blueprint: How Med Spas Doing $500K to $2M Add 50 Paying Clients in 90 Days Without Buying Another Course**

**Alternates to split-test in ad creative:**
- The Revenue Leak Masterclass: Why Your Med Spa Doesn't Have a Lead Problem
- The $200,000 You Already Earned and Never Collected
- Course Fatigue: What to Do After the Fifth Program Didn't Work

The title carries the course-fatigue angle, which is already the primary positioning for paid traffic. It does double duty here: it names the pain and it pre-frames why a done-with-you partnership is different from the programs they already bought.

## 1.2 Who this is built for

Independent med spa owners doing $500K to $2M annually. Typically owner-operated, often an injector or an RN who built a book of business and then hit a ceiling. They have bought at least one program, course, or coaching container that did not stick. They are busy in the treatment room, not the CEO seat.

## 1.3 The single big idea

**You do not have a lead problem. You have a leak problem. And no course will ever fix a leak, because information does not install.**

Every teaching segment, every ad, every email, and the pitch itself ladder up to that one sentence. If an attendee remembers nothing else, they should remember that.

## 1.4 The conversion architecture (decide this before you build the page)

You have two viable paths. I recommend Path A.

**Path A: Dual-CTA (recommended)**
- Primary close on the call: apply for a Growth Partnership Blueprint Call. Limited seats, application-gated.
- Secondary close for everyone who is not ready: the $29 Revenue Leak Audit with KPI Calculator.

This is the strongest structure for a $9,000 to $15,000 offer, because the $29 audit converts the 80 percent who will never book a call from a cold webinar, and the audit itself is the natural on-ramp to the Blueprint Call two weeks later. Nobody leaves empty-handed, and nobody leaves un-monetized.

**Path B: Single-CTA to application only**
Cleaner and higher perceived value, but you leave the majority of the room unconverted and you rebuild the same audience from scratch next month.

**Recommendation: run Path A.** Pitch the partnership first at full conviction, then present the $29 audit as the "start smaller" door rather than as a discount. Never let the audit read as a consolation prize. Frame it as step one of the same methodology.

## 1.5 Benchmarks to hold yourself to

| Metric | Acceptable | Good | Excellent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ad click-through rate | 1.0% | 1.8% | 2.5%+ |
| Registration page conversion | 25% | 35% | 45%+ |
| Cost per registration | $18 | $12 | $8 |
| Show-up rate (live) | 25% | 35% | 45%+ |
| Stay-to-pitch rate | 50% | 65% | 75%+ |
| $29 audit take rate (of attendees) | 8% | 15% | 22%+ |
| Applications booked (of attendees) | 3% | 6% | 10%+ |
| Application to closed partnership | 15% | 25% | 35%+ |

Run the math on your own numbers before you spend a dollar. At 200 registrations, a 35 percent show rate, and a 6 percent application rate, you are booking roughly 4 calls per webinar. At a 25 percent close on a $9,000 partnership, that is one client per event, plus the audit revenue and the follow-up conversions. That is a profitable machine only if you run it weekly, so build it to be repeatable, not perfect.

---

# PART 2: THE META AD CAMPAIGN

## 2.1 Campaign structure

- **Objective:** Leads (on-site conversion, Lead event fired on registration confirmation)
- **Budget:** Start at $60 to $100 per day for 7 days before judging anything
- **Campaign:** One campaign, Advantage+ audience with a lookalike or interest seed
- **Ad sets:**
  1. Broad, age 30 to 60, women 75 percent weighted, US, Advantage+ placements
  2. Interest stack: Botox, dermal filler, medical spa, Allergan, Galderma, aesthetic practice, med spa owner, American Med Spa Association
  3. Retargeting: website visitors 180 days, Instagram and Facebook engagers 365 days, client list lookalike 1 percent
- **Creative per ad set:** 3 to 4 variations minimum. Kill anything under a 1 percent CTR after 1,000 impressions.

**Best-performing creative formats for this audience, in order:** talking-head video shot on your phone in the treatment room or office, static text-on-image quote card, carousel of the five leaks, screen recording of the KPI calculator.

## 2.2 Ad 1: The Course Fatigue angle (lead with this one)

**Primary text:**

You have bought the course. You have joined the group. You have the folder of PDFs you never opened.

And your revenue is roughly where it was 18 months ago.

That is not a discipline problem. It is a structural one. Courses hand you information. Information does not install itself into a business that is already running at capacity, staffed by people who did not attend the course, in a market you never actually mapped.

I am running a free 60-minute class for med spa owners doing $500K to $2M.

Inside, I am going to show you the five places your revenue leaks out before it ever reaches your bank account, the math that tells you whether you have a lead problem or a leak problem, and what actually has to get installed to add 50 paying clients in 90 days.

No pitch for another course. I do not sell one.

Save your seat below. Replay goes to registrants only.

**Headline:** The Class for Owners Who Are Done Buying Courses
**Description:** Free 60-minute masterclass for med spas doing $500K to $2M
**CTA button:** Sign Up

## 2.3 Ad 2: The Leak Math angle

**Primary text:**

Quick math for any med spa owner reading this.

100 leads come in this month. 42 book a consult. 30 actually show. 13 buy. 4 ever come back.

Change one number: consult close rate from 43 percent to 60 percent. Nothing else. No extra ad spend, no new leads, no new staff.

That single change is worth six figures a year to most practices at your size.

Now stack four more changes like it.

That is the entire class. 60 minutes, free, for med spa owners doing $500K to $2M. I will walk the numbers live and give you the calculator I use with clients.

Seat link below.

**Headline:** Your Med Spa Doesn't Have a Lead Problem
**Description:** The 5 revenue leaks costing you six figures a year

## 2.4 Ad 3: The Identity angle

**Primary text:**

You opened this practice because you were good at the thing.

Then you became the marketing department, the HR department, the front desk backup, the inventory manager, and the person who stays until 9pm rebuilding the schedule.

The spa you imagined is still in there. So are you.

I am teaching a free 60-minute class for med spa owners doing $500K to $2M on exactly what has to get installed to get both of those back: the systems, the sales training, the membership architecture, the follow-up that runs without you.

Not theory. The actual install list, in order, with the numbers behind it.

Link below.

**Headline:** The Spa You Imagined Is Still In There
**Description:** Free masterclass for independent med spa owners

## 2.5 Ad 4: Short-form video script (45 to 60 seconds, phone camera)

> Hey, if you own a med spa doing somewhere between five hundred thousand and two million a year, I want thirty seconds.
>
> I've audited a lot of practices at your size, and I'll tell you what I almost never find. I almost never find a lead problem.
>
> What I find is a spa that's paying to generate a lead, and then losing that lead in the gap between the inquiry and the booking. Or losing them at the consult. Or converting them once and never seeing them again.
>
> You're not underperforming because you don't know enough. You're underperforming because nothing's installed.
>
> So I'm running a free class. One hour. I'm going to show you the five leaks, I'm going to show you the math on each one, and I'm going to show you the exact order to fix them in.
>
> It's free. There's no course at the end, because I don't sell courses. Link's right here. Come find your money.

## 2.6 Registration page (above the fold)

**Headline:** Your Med Spa Doesn't Have a Lead Problem. It Has a Leak Problem.

**Subhead:** A free 60-minute class for independent med spa owners doing $500K to $2M: the five places your revenue disappears, the math behind each one, and the exact install order to add 50 paying clients in 90 days.

**Bullets (what you will walk away with):**
- The Revenue Leak Audit framework, the same one used to open every client engagement
- The KPI math that tells you in ten minutes whether you have a lead problem or a leak problem
- Why the last three programs you bought did not move revenue, and what the missing layer actually is
- The install order for memberships, packages, follow-up, and staff sales training, and why doing them out of order wastes the effort
- The capacity ceiling calculation most owners have never run on their own practice

**Form:** First name, email, mobile, practice name, annual revenue range (dropdown). Keep it to five fields. The revenue dropdown is your best qualification signal and your best segmentation tool for follow-up.

**Below the form:** one line of proof, a photograph of you, and a single sentence of bio. Nothing else. Long registration pages reduce registrations.

---

# PART 3: SHOW-UP SEQUENCE

Registration is not the goal. Attendance is. Budget as much attention to this sequence as to the ads.

| Timing | Channel | Message |
|---|---|---|
| Immediately | Email | Confirmation, calendar link, and one assignment: pull last month's lead count, consult count, and close count before the class. "Bring three numbers." |
| 24 hours after registration | Email | The "why this is different" email. Course fatigue story, short. |
| 1 day before | Email + SMS | Reminder plus a preview of one leak, with the number attached. |
| 2 hours before | SMS | "We start at 12. Bring your three numbers. Here's your link." |
| 10 minutes before | Email + SMS | Door is open. Come early, I answer questions in the first five minutes. |
| At start time | SMS | We are live. Link. |

The homework assignment is the highest-leverage element in this entire sequence. An attendee who brings their own numbers is participating in the teaching rather than watching it, and participants convert at multiples of spectators.

# PART 4: THE 60-MINUTE RUN OF SHOW

| Minutes | Segment | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00 to 0:05 | Open loop and rules of engagement | Hook, set the promise, get first chat interaction |
| 0:05 to 0:10 | Origin and credibility | Earn the right to teach without a resume dump |
| 0:10 to 0:14 | The Big Domino | Establish leak over lead, the one belief everything hangs on |
| 0:14 to 0:27 | Teaching Block 1: The Five Leaks | Deliver the Revenue Leak Audit framework with live math |

| 0:43 to 0:45 | The Bridge | Transition from teaching to offer without a tonal cliff |
| 0:45 to 0:56 | The Offer | Stack, guarantee, price, scarcity, close |
| 0:56 to 1:00+ | Q&A that closes | Objection handling live, second and third close |

Hold the timing. The single most common failure in a first webinar is spending 40 minutes on teaching block one and rushing the offer. Rehearse with a timer twice before you go live.

# PART 5: WORD-FOR-WORD SCRIPTS

## 5.1 The Open (0:00 to 0:05)

> Alright, we're live. Give me a quick one in the chat: your first name and the city your practice is in. I want to see who's here.
>
> While those come in, let me tell you exactly what the next sixty minutes are.

I'm going to do the math on each one, live, using real numbers from real med spas doing what you're doing. And I'm going to show you the order you have to fix them in, because the order matters more than almost anything else and almost nobody gets it right.

>

>
> One: be here. Close the other tab. I know you can multitask, I know you're probably between patients. But I promise you the money in this hour is worth an hour, and I've watched too many owners half-watch this and miss the number that would've changed their year.

>
> Okay. Let's go find your money.

## 5.2 Origin and Credibility (0:05 to 0:10)

> Quick on me, and I'll keep it short, because your time is better spent on the frameworks than on my resume.
>
> I'm Bethany. I'm the co-founder and CEO of The Luxora Collective. We're a revenue growth partner for independent med spas, and specifically for practices doing roughly five hundred thousand to two million a year, which is the hardest, loneliest revenue band in this entire industry.

> Here's why it's the hardest. Under five hundred thousand, everything is a hustle problem, and hustle solves it. Over three or four million, you have infrastructure. You have a director of operations, you have a marketing person, you have a real front desk team.
>
> But between five hundred thousand and two million, you're the bottleneck. You're the injector, you're the marketing department, you're the person fixing the schedule at nine at night, and you're the reason the practice works. Which also means you're the ceiling.
>
> I want to tell you the thing that made me build this business the way I built it.
>
> I kept meeting owners who had bought everything. The eight thousand dollar coaching program. The course with the Facebook group. The mastermind with the retreat. Smart, hardworking women, with folders full of material they never implemented, feeling like the problem was them.
>
> It was not them.
>
> Information transfers. Implementation doesn't. When somebody hands you a curriculum and walks away, they've transferred the burden of installation onto the busiest person in the building. That's not education. That's a very expensive to-do list.
>
> So we built the opposite. We don't teach and leave. We audit, we blueprint, and then we install, with you, alongside your team, until it's running. And we do it with full knowledge transfer, because my actual goal is that at the end of our year together you're more capable and more in control, not more dependent on me. If you need me forever, I did it wrong.
>
> That's the philosophy. Now let me show you the framework.

## 5.3 The Big Domino (0:10 to 0:14)

> I need to change one belief in the next four minutes, and if I do, the rest of this hour is going to land completely differently.
>
> Here's the belief. Most owners at your size think they have a lead problem.
>
> "If I could just get more leads." "I need to figure out Instagram." "Should I be doing TikTok?" "My ads guy isn't performing."
>
> I've now looked inside a lot of practices in this revenue band, and I'll be honest with you: I almost never find a lead problem. I find a leak problem.
>
> Here's what a leak problem looks like. You pay to generate a hundred inquiries. Forty-two of them book something. Thirty actually show up. Thirteen buy. And four of those thirteen ever come back.
>
> Do you see what happened? You paid for a hundred and you monetized thirteen, and then you retained four. You didn't have a traffic problem. You had five separate points where money walked out of the building, and every single one of them was fixable without spending another dollar on ads.
>
> And here's the brutal part, the part that I need you to sit with for a second.
>
> When you pour more leads into a leaking system, you don't grow. You just leak faster. And it costs more to do it.
>
> That's why the ads didn't work. That's why the course didn't work. Not because the tactics were wrong. Because you applied traffic tactics to a conversion and retention problem.
>
> So here's my promise for the next thirty minutes. I'm going to show you every leak, I'm going to price it, and I'm going to give you the order to plug them in.
>
> Type LEAK in the chat if that lands. I want to know you're with me.

## 5.4 Teaching Block 1: The Five Leaks (0:14 to 0:27)

> Okay. This is the Revenue Leak Audit. It's the first thing we do with every client we take on, before we touch marketing, before we spend a dollar, before we recommend anything. And I'm going to give you the whole framework right now.
>
> Five leaks. Get your three numbers ready.
>
> **Leak one. Speed to lead.**
>
> Somebody fills out your form at 7:40 on a Tuesday evening. When does a human being contact them?
>
> For most practices at your size, the honest answer is the next morning, if it's a good week. Sometimes two days.
>
> Response inside five minutes versus response the next day is a multiple, not a percentage. That lead's intent is highest in the first ten minutes and it decays fast, and while you're sleeping they're filling out the form for the practice two miles away who has automated follow-up running.
>
> This is the cheapest leak to fix and it's the one that's leaking right now, tonight, while you're on this call.
>
> **Leak two. The consult close rate.**
>
> This is the big one. This is where the six figures are.
>
> Somebody walks into your building. They took time off work. They're sitting in front of you. And a huge number of practices at your size close somewhere between forty and fifty percent of those.
>
> Let's price it. Say you run thirty consults a month at an average first purchase of twelve hundred dollars. At forty-five percent, that's about sixteen thousand a month. At sixty-five percent, that's twenty-three thousand a month. Same consults. Same room. Same you.
>
> That gap is about eighty-five thousand dollars a year, and the only thing that changed was that somebody on your team was trained to have a structured conversation instead of an enthusiastic one.
>
> And here's what I want to say carefully, because I know how this lands for a lot of you. Most owners in aesthetics were never trained to sell, and a lot of you actively don't want to be salespeople. I understand that completely. But a patient who wanted the outcome, could afford the outcome, and walked out without it because nobody guided the conversation, that isn't ethics. That's a failure of service.
>
> **Leak three. The one-and-done.**
>
> Here's the number that changes practices. It costs somewhere between five and seven times more to acquire a new patient than to bring an existing one back.
>
> And the average med spa at your size has a database of hundreds or thousands of people who purchased once, had a great experience, and simply were never contacted again in any structured way.
>
> That database is the single most valuable asset in your business, and for most of you it is currently doing absolutely nothing.
>
> **Leak four. No rebooking at the point of exit.**
>
> Your patient is at the front desk. They're glowing. They love you. It's the highest-emotion moment in the entire experience.
>
> And your front desk says, "we'll send you a reminder."
>
> You just handed the most persuadable person in your building over to their own calendar, their own memory, and their own budget three months from now. Rebooking at exit, as a required step, with the next appointment scheduled before they walk out, is a structural change that costs you nothing and lifts retention immediately.
>
> **Leak five. No recurring revenue.**
>
> Every month you start at zero.
>
> That's the actual source of the anxiety, by the way. Not the revenue number. The starting over. The first of the month arrives and the number is zero and you have to go get it again, and you've been doing that for years.
>
> A properly structured membership changes the shape of the business. Not a discount club, which is what most med spa memberships actually are, and which quietly destroys margin. A membership designed around a treatment cadence you want anyway, priced against lifetime value, with a retail attachment.
>
> That's leak five, and it's the one that changes how the business feels to run, not just what it earns.
>
> Now stack all five. Ten percent recovered here, fifteen there, a membership base, a reactivated database. For a practice doing a million dollars, this is routinely a two to four hundred thousand dollar swing, and none of it required a single additional lead.
>
> Drop a number in the chat: which leak is bleeding hardest in your practice right now? One through five.

## 5.5 Teaching Block 2: The Blueprint (0:27 to 0:35)

> So you know where the leaks are. Here's the step almost nobody runs, and it's the reason a lot of well-executed marketing money gets set on fire.
>
> Before you invest another dollar in growth, you need a blueprint. Three calculations.
>
> **Calculation one: your capacity ceiling.**
>
> How much revenue can your practice physically produce with the rooms, the devices, and the providers you have right now?
>
> Treatment rooms, times operating hours, times realistic utilization, times your average hourly production. Run it.
>
> The reason this matters is that I've watched owners spend fifteen thousand dollars a month on ads to fill a schedule that was already at eighty-five percent of physical capacity. There was no room for the growth they were buying. They were paying to create a waitlist, and then patients were leaving because they couldn't get in for six weeks.
>
> If you're near your ceiling, your growth strategy isn't more leads. It's raising your average ticket, changing your service mix toward higher-margin treatments, or adding capacity. Completely different plan, and no ad agency on earth is going to tell you that, because it isn't what they sell.
>
> **Calculation two: your real lifetime value.**
>
> Not first purchase. Lifetime. Average purchase, times purchases per year, times years retained.
>
> Most owners have never calculated this, and it's the number that governs every other decision you'll make. It tells you what you can afford to pay for a patient. It tells you what your membership should cost. It tells you whether that eight hundred dollar acquisition cost is insane or a bargain.
>
> If your LTV is nine hundred dollars, a two hundred dollar acquisition cost is a problem. If your LTV is forty-two hundred, it's the best trade in your business and you should be doing more of it immediately.
>
> **Calculation three: your market reality.**
>
> How many practices within your radius offer what you offer? What do they charge? What does your population actually support?
>
> Because if you're the ninth injector in a three-mile radius, competing on price is a death sentence, and your blueprint has to be built around differentiation and experience rather than volume.
>
> Those three calculations together are what we call the Market Blueprint, and we build it for every client before we recommend a single investment. It's the difference between a growth plan and a guess.
>
> Here's the discipline I'd ask you to hold, even if you never work with us: **never spend money on growth before you've run the blueprint.** Audit, then blueprint, then invest. In that order. Every time.

## 5.6 Teaching Block 3: The Growth Engine (0:35 to 0:43)

> Last block, and this is the one I want to be very direct about.
>
> You now know the leaks. You know the blueprint. So why isn't this already fixed? Because you're smart, you're capable, and I guarantee you've heard pieces of this before.
>
> Here's why. And it's not a motivation problem.
>
> Everything I just described has to get installed. Installed means: written into an SOP, trained into your team, built into your software, measured on a dashboard, and enforced by someone whose job it is to enforce it.
>
> A course cannot do that. A course hands you the knowledge and then leaves the installation to the single busiest person in the building, who is also the person generating most of the revenue by being in the treatment room. That's why the folder is still unopened. Not because you're lazy. Because you were sold information when you needed installation.
>
> Here's the actual install list, in order. Write this down.
>
> One: audit and blueprint. Know your leaks, know your ceiling, know your LTV.
>
> Two: sales training for every client-facing person. This is first, because it multiplies everything downstream. Every lead you generate afterward is worth more.
>
> Three: systems and SOPs. Speed to lead, follow-up automation, rebooking at exit, your CRM actually configured to do the work instead of just storing names.
>
> Four: revenue architecture. Memberships, package structure, retail as a real profit center rather than a shelf of product nobody sells.
>
> Five: reputation engine. Systematic review generation, because in aesthetics your reviews are your ad budget's efficiency multiplier.
>
> Six: acquisition. Ads, partnerships, events, referral systems. This is last. Last. Because now every dollar you spend enters a system that converts and retains, instead of a bucket with five holes in it.
>
> And if it matters to your patient base, there's a longevity and wellness layer, peptides, hormones, GLP-1 support, that fits on top of this. Optional, not core.
>
> Look at that order again. Notice where acquisition sits. Sixth.

> Then we install the **Growth Engine**, with you. Here's what that includes.

> **Team infrastructure.** Compensation and incentive design, so your people are paid in a way that pulls in the same direction as your revenue goals, plus hiring and onboarding structure.
>
> **Acquisition management.** Paid ads, run by us, on your account. Partnerships, referral systems, events. And this comes last, on purpose, because now it works.

>

> Every single thing we install, we transfer. Your team learns to run it. Because the goal is that in a year, you're a more capable operator with a more valuable business, not a person on a retainer who can't function without me. If you need me forever, I've failed.

# PART 6: Q&A THAT CLOSES (0:56 to end)

Q&A is not an epilogue. It is your second and third close, and it is where undecided attendees convert. Never end the moment questions run out. Seed your own questions if the chat is quiet.

**Structure every answer in three beats:** answer the question honestly, tell a 20-second client story that proves the answer, then return to the link.

## Seeded questions to have ready

**"How fast do people see results?"**
> Honest answer: the sales training and speed-to-lead fixes move numbers inside two to three weeks, because you're converting traffic you already have. Memberships and reputation compound over sixty to ninety days. Acquisition is last and it's the slowest, which is exactly why we don't start there. Anybody promising you thirty days on everything is selling you something.

**"I've already got a marketing agency."**
> Great, keep them if they're good. We're not the same thing. Your agency's job is to bring people to the door. Ours is to make sure the building doesn't leak. Honestly, if you fix the leaks, your agency's numbers get better and they look like heroes. If your agency is underperforming, that usually shows up in the blueprint pretty fast, and we'll tell you.

**"My team won't buy in."**
> That's the most common real objection and it's a legitimate one. Two things. First, this is why the compensation and incentive work exists: when your team's pay is structured so the changes make them money, resistance drops enormously. Second, we do the training. It's not you walking into a staff meeting alone with new rules. It's an outside expert setting a new standard, which is a completely different dynamic and you know it is.

**"Is this just for injectors?"**
> No. This works for any practice with consults, treatment plans, and repeat visits. Lasers, body contouring, wellness, hormone practices. The five leaks are structural. The service mix changes the math, not the framework.

**"Why is it so expensive?"** (Ask this one yourself if nobody does.)
> Fair question. Compare it to what it replaces. A director of operations who could install a fraction of this is ninety thousand a year plus benefits. A sales trainer is a five-figure engagement on its own. A decent agency is four to eight thousand a month with no operational work at all. And compare it to the leaks. If your consult close rate is costing you eighty-five thousand a year, and it is for most practices this size, the partnership pays for itself before we finish the install. The expensive option is the one where nothing changes for another year.

**"What if it doesn't work for me?"**
> That's what the Premium tier's guarantee is for, in writing. And it's what the Blueprint Call is for. If I don't think we can produce a return for you, I'll tell you on that call and I won't take your money. I'd rather have a clean no than a bad client.

## The final close

> We're at time. Two links, one last time.
>
> If you know, apply for the Blueprint Call. Three spots.
>
> If you're not there yet, take the twenty-nine dollar Revenue Leak Audit. Everyone should do that one.
>
> And if you do neither, please do this: run the five leaks on your own practice this week. Write the dollar number next to each one. That exercise alone is worth the hour you gave me, and you deserve to know what those numbers are.
>
> Thank you for your time. It's the most expensive thing you own and you spent an hour of it with me. I don't take that lightly. Go find your money.

---

# PART 7: POST-EVENT EMAIL CADENCE

Built on Ashley's post-event cadence structure, adapted for this webinar. Segment on day two by behavior: attendees who bought the audit, attendees who did not, and no-shows.

| Day | Segment | Subject | Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0, within 2 hours | All attendees | The links from today's class | Replay for 48 hours, both CTAs, one-paragraph recap of the five leaks. Short. |
| 0 | No-shows | You missed it, here's one thing | Deliver the single highest-value leak in full. Replay access for 24 hours only. Both links. |
| 1 | Non-buyers | The leak nobody wants to talk about | Full teardown of the consult close rate leak with the math. Ends on the $29 audit. |
| 2 | Non-buyers | What Monday looks like | The implementation gap. Course fatigue story. Ends on the Blueprint Call application. |
| 3 | Non-buyers | 50 clients in 90 days, in writing | The guarantee explained in detail, including the contingencies, because transparency about the contingencies increases belief rather than reducing it. |
| 4 | Non-buyers | Objection email | The three reasons owners say no, answered directly. Price, timing, team buy-in. |
| 5 | Non-buyers | Replay is coming down | Final urgency. Both links. Spots remaining. |
| 7 | Audit buyers | Your audit, and what to do with it | Delivery plus the natural upgrade path to the Blueprint Call. This is your highest-converting segment. Give it the most attention. |
| 10 | All non-buyers | The one calculation | Pure value. Capacity ceiling walkthrough. Rebuilds goodwill and re-engages openers for the next event. |
| 14 | All non-buyers | Invitation to the next class | Roll them into the next webinar cohort. Never let a registrant list go cold. |

Two rules for this sequence. First, every email delivers something usable even if the reader never buys, because your list is a long-term asset and burning it for one launch is expensive. Second, the audit-buyer segment is your warmest revenue: those people paid you money and self-identified. Call them, do not just email them.

---

# PART 8: TECH, TEAM, AND CHECKLIST

## Stack
- **Platform:** Zoom Webinar or StreamYard into a custom page. Avoid platforms that make attendees install anything.
- **Registration and follow-up:** GHL, with the revenue-range field mapped to a segmentation tag from the start.
- **Slides:** Roughly 30 to 40. Mostly one number or one sentence per slide. No paragraphs. The leak math slides should build one line at a time.
- **Chat moderator:** Aanchal or a team member, in the chat the whole time, dropping links on cue, answering logistics, flagging good questions and buying signals for you. This role is worth real money and is routinely skipped.

## Pre-flight checklist
1. Run the full script out loud with a timer, twice. Adjust to fit 60 minutes with 5 minutes of slack.
2. Pull three real client leak examples with actual dollar figures to use in Block 1. Anonymized. Specificity is the whole game.
3. Have both links pre-written in a text file so the moderator can paste instantly.
4. Confirm the application form and the $29 checkout both work on mobile. Test them on your own phone.
5. Decide the real number of partnership spots before you go live and never say a number you will not honor.
6. Set the replay window and enforce it.
7. Record everything. The first three runs are rehearsal for the evergreen version.

## After three live runs
Take the highest-converting recording, cut it into an evergreen replay funnel, and run cold traffic to it continuously. Keep one live event monthly for fresh material and testimonials. The live version is where the offer gets sharpened. The evergreen version is where it scales.

# The Luxora Collective
## The 60-Minute Masterclass System (v2: Emotional Positioning)
### Ad campaign, run of show, word-for-word scripts, pitch, and follow-up cadence

> **What changed from v1:** the course-fatigue angle is retired. Med spa owners at this level are not course buyers and do not identify with that pain. Every ad, every script beat, and the offer itself now runs on the emotional problem they are actually living with: money that disappears, a business that owns them, a team they cannot trust, and the quiet fear that they will fail after everyone believed in them. The tactical frameworks stay. They are now the proof, not the promise.

---

# PART 1: THE STRATEGIC FRAME

## 1.1 The positioning rule

**Sell the emotional outcome. Prove it with the mechanism. Never lead with the mechanism.**

Owners do not want a CRM, an audit, better ads, or AI follow-up. They want predictable revenue, a team they can trust, patients who come back, and a practice that does not require them to be in the building. Everything in this document leads with the second list and proves it with the first.

The reframe in one line: **you do not have a revenue problem, you have a revenue that requires you problem.**

## 1.2 The working title

**Primary title:**
> **The $100K Month With Nothing Left: How Med Spa Owners Build Revenue That's Predictable, a Team That Sells Without Them, and a Practice They Can Actually Leave**

**Alternates to split-test:**
- Owned By Your Own Business: The 60-Minute Class for Med Spa Owners Who Can't Take a Vacation
- Where Did The Money Go? A Live Class on Profit, Payroll, and the $100K Month That Left You Broke
- The Practice That Doesn't Need You
- Predictable: How to Stop Starting Every Month at Zero

**Why the primary wins:** it is the sentence they have said in their own head, and it names all three deliverables in the subhead. It also self-qualifies. An owner who has never had a $100K month is not the buyer.

## 1.3 The three promises of the class

Every med spa owner at this level is carrying nine pains. You cannot address nine things in an hour. Cluster them into three, and each teaching block resolves one:

| Block | Emotional pain it resolves | What they leave with |
|---|---|---|
| 1. The Money | Financial fear, decision fatigue, marketing frustration | Where the money actually went, and the three numbers that end the guessing |
| 2. The Team | Team distrust, staffing churn, being the only closer | Why nobody sells like them, and what has to change so someone does |
| 3. The Return | Retention, feeling trapped, unpredictable months | How to build revenue that shows up before the month starts |

The fourth pain cluster, fear of failure and comparison, is never taught. It is named once in the origin story and once in the bridge. Name it, do not dwell on it, and never exploit it.

## 1.4 Who this is for

Independent med spa owners doing $500K to $2M annually. Usually the top producer in their own building. Often invested savings, sometimes leveraged their home, frequently left a stable clinical career. They are not lazy, uninformed, or unmotivated. They are at capacity, and every problem in the practice routes through one person.

**Tone rule for the entire funnel:** never condescend, never imply they did it wrong, never speak to them like a student. Speak to them like a peer who has seen inside forty practices that look exactly like theirs. Their situation is structural, not personal, and every line of copy should carry that.

## 1.5 The conversion architecture

**Dual CTA. Recommended and unchanged from v1.**

- **Primary:** apply for a Blueprint Call. Application-gated, limited spots.
- **Secondary:** the $29 Revenue Leak Audit with KPI Calculator, framed as "find out where your money went" rather than as a discount or a downsell.

The $29 audit maps perfectly onto the new positioning, because financial fear is the strongest of the nine pains and the audit is the direct answer to it. Position it as the cheapest way to stop guessing, not as a smaller version of the partnership.

## 1.6 Benchmarks

| Metric | Acceptable | Good | Excellent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ad click-through rate | 1.0% | 1.8% | 2.5%+ |
| Registration page conversion | 25% | 35% | 45%+ |
| Cost per registration | $18 | $12 | $8 |
| Show-up rate (live) | 25% | 35% | 45%+ |
| Stay-to-pitch rate | 50% | 65% | 75%+ |
| $29 audit take rate (of attendees) | 8% | 15% | 22%+ |
| Applications booked (of attendees) | 3% | 6% | 10%+ |
| Application to closed partnership | 15% | 25% | 35%+ |

At 200 registrations, a 35 percent show rate, and a 6 percent application rate, you book roughly 4 calls per event. This is a weekly or biweekly machine, not a one-time launch. Build it to repeat.

---

# PART 2: THE META AD CAMPAIGN

## 2.1 Campaign structure

- **Objective:** Leads, on-site conversion, Lead event on registration confirmation
- **Budget:** $60 to $100 per day minimum, 7 days before judging anything
- **Ad sets:**
  1. Broad, ages 30 to 60, weighted female, US, Advantage+ placements
  2. Interest stack: medical spa, Botox, dermal filler, Allergan, Galderma, aesthetic practice ownership, American Med Spa Association, practice management
  3. Retargeting: 180-day site visitors, 365-day IG and FB engagers, 1 percent lookalike from client list
- **Creative per set:** 3 to 4 minimum. Kill anything under 1 percent CTR after 1,000 impressions.

**Creative note:** the highest-performing format for this audience is you, on a phone camera, saying a sentence they have said to themselves. Production value actively hurts here. It reads as agency, and agency is one of their pains.

## 2.2 Ad 1: Financial fear (lead with this one)

**Primary text:**

You had a hundred thousand dollar month.

Then payroll cleared. Then the product invoice. Then the ad spend, the rent, the merchant fees, the device lease.

And you sat there looking at your account thinking: where did it go? I did everything right. Why does this still feel tight?

Here is the part nobody says out loud. Revenue and money are not the same thing, and a practice can grow revenue for three straight years while the owner takes home less every year.

I am teaching a free 60-minute class for med spa owners doing $500K to $2M on exactly where that money goes and how to get it back. Not theory. Live math, on the same three numbers I run on every practice I work with.

Bring last month's numbers. You will leave knowing what your practice is actually keeping and what it should be.

Seat link below.

**Headline:** A $100K Month Shouldn't Feel Like This
**Description:** Free class for med spa owners doing $500K to $2M
**CTA:** Sign Up

## 2.3 Ad 2: Trapped and freedom

**Primary text:**

When was your last real vacation? Not the one where you answered texts from the pool.

You built this practice to have more control over your life. Instead you built a job that cannot run for four days without you.

If you stop, revenue stops. Every emergency lands on your desk. The schedule falls apart when you are not the one holding it. And somewhere in there you stopped being the owner and became the highest-paid employee of a business you happen to own.

That is not a work ethic problem. It is a structural one, and it is fixable.

Free 60-minute class for med spa owners doing $500K to $2M: how to build predictable revenue, a team that sells when you are not in the room, and patients who come back without you chasing them.

Link below. Come with your numbers.

**Headline:** You Own a Business That Owns You
**Description:** The class on building a practice that runs without you

## 2.4 Ad 3: Team and staffing

**Primary text:**

Be honest. Nobody in your building sells like you do.

Your front desk does not follow up. Your providers do not educate the patient on what comes next. Everybody is "slammed," and yet the consult that should have closed at three thousand walked out at four hundred.

So you step in. Again. And now you are the injector, the closer, the trainer, and the person rebuilding the schedule at nine at night.

Then the injector you finally trained leaves and takes half her patients with her.

I am running a free 60-minute class for med spa owners doing $500K to $2M. One full section is on this exact problem: why your team does not sell, why it is almost never a hiring problem, and what has to change in training and compensation before anybody performs the way you need them to.

Link below.

**Headline:** Nobody Sells Like You. That's the Problem.
**Description:** Free class on building a med spa team you can trust

## 2.5 Ad 4: Retention

**Primary text:**

You spent three hundred dollars to get her in the door.

She loved her results. She hugged you on the way out. She told two friends.

And you have not seen her in fourteen months.

That is the most expensive thing happening in your practice right now, and it does not show up anywhere on your P&L. It just quietly shows up as a slow month you cannot explain.

Free 60-minute class for med spa owners doing $500K to $2M: how to build revenue that repeats, so you stop starting every month at zero and stop paying full price for patients you already earned.

Link below.

**Headline:** She Came Once and Never Came Back
**Description:** The retention math costing med spas six figures a year

## 2.6 Ad 5: Video script, 45 to 60 seconds, phone camera

> If you own a med spa doing somewhere between five hundred thousand and two million a year, I want to say something to you that you probably haven't said out loud.
>
> You're working harder than you've ever worked in your life. And you open Instagram and everybody else looks like they're crushing it. And there's this thought in the back of your head that goes: what am I doing wrong? Why is this so hard for me?
>
> I've been inside a lot of practices at your size. I'll tell you exactly what I find.
>
> I find an owner who is the best salesperson, the best injector, the marketing department, and the safety net, all at once. And there's no version of that where the business gets easier. It just gets heavier.
>
> That's not a you problem. Nobody ever installed anything. You've been holding it up personally, for years.
>
> I'm teaching a free class. One hour. Where your money's actually going, why your team doesn't sell the way you do, and how to build revenue that shows up whether or not you're in the building.
>
> Link's right here. Bring last month's numbers.

## 2.7 Registration page

**Headline:** You Had a $100K Month. So Where Did the Money Go?

**Subhead:** A free 60-minute class for independent med spa owners doing $500K to $2M: how to build revenue that's predictable, a team that sells when you're not in the room, and a practice you could actually leave for a week.

**Section: This class is for you if you've ever thought...**
- "I made more this year and somehow I'm taking home less."
- "I can't take a vacation. If I stop, the revenue stops."
- "Nobody here sells the way I do."
- "I've spent tens of thousands on agencies and I still don't know what's working."
- "She bought once, loved it, and I never saw her again."
- "I'm exhausted from making forty decisions a day with no one to check them against."

**Section: What you'll walk out with**
- The three numbers that tell you where your money is actually going, and how to run them in ten minutes
- Why your team does not sell like you do, and the two structural changes that fix it faster than hiring
- The retention architecture that turns one-time patients into predictable monthly revenue
- The capacity ceiling calculation that determines whether more marketing will help you or bury you
- A clear order of operations, so you stop making forty isolated decisions a month

**Form:** first name, email, mobile, practice name, annual revenue range. Five fields, no more. Revenue range drives segmentation.

**Below the form:** your photo, one sentence of bio, one line of proof. Nothing else.

---

# PART 3: SHOW-UP SEQUENCE

| Timing | Channel | Message |
|---|---|---|
| Immediately | Email | Confirmation, calendar link, and the assignment: last month's total revenue, what you personally took home, lead count, consult count, close count. "Bring five numbers. This becomes an audit of your practice instead of a class." |
| 24 hours after | Email | The "you are not doing it wrong" email. Short, personal, names the comparison pain. |
| 1 day before | Email + SMS | Reminder plus one preview insight with a real dollar figure attached |
| 2 hours before | SMS | "We start at 12. Bring your numbers." |
| 10 minutes before | Email + SMS | Doors open, come early, I answer questions first |
| At start | SMS | Live now, link |

The homework is the highest-leverage element in the funnel. An owner who brings her own numbers stops being an audience member. Participants convert at multiples of spectators.

---

# PART 4: THE 60-MINUTE RUN OF SHOW

| Minutes | Segment | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00 to 0:05 | Open, promise, rules | Hook on the emotional problem, get first chat interaction |
| 0:05 to 0:11 | Origin and permission | Earn trust, remove shame, name fear of failure once |
| 0:11 to 0:15 | The Big Domino | Revenue that requires you is not an asset |
| 0:15 to 0:27 | Block 1: The Money | Financial fear resolved with live math |
| 0:27 to 0:36 | Block 2: The Team | Team distrust and staffing resolved structurally |
| 0:36 to 0:44 | Block 3: The Return | Retention and predictability, ends on freedom |
| 0:44 to 0:46 | The Bridge | Decision fatigue and capacity, honest transition |
| 0:46 to 0:57 | The Offer | Stack, guarantee, price, scarcity, close |
| 0:57 to end | Q&A that closes | Live objection handling, second and third close |

Rehearse with a timer twice. The most common failure is overrunning block one and rushing the offer.

---

# PART 5: WORD-FOR-WORD SCRIPTS

> Delivery note: these are spoken scripts. Read them out loud, not with your eyes. Where the language feels stiff in your mouth, change it. Your delivery beats my wording every time. Slow down on the emotional lines. The instinct is to rush past them because they feel heavy. That heaviness is the reason they work.

## 5.1 The Open (0:00 to 0:05)

> Alright, we're live. Do me a favor: first name and the city your practice is in, in the chat. I want to see who's here.
>
> While those come in, let me tell you what the next sixty minutes are.
>
> I'm going to answer three questions. Where is your money actually going. Why doesn't anybody on your team sell the way you do. And how do you build a practice that keeps producing when you're not standing in it.
>
> That's it. Those three.
>
> And I'm going to do it with real math, on real numbers, from practices that look exactly like yours.
>
> Here's what this isn't. This is not a hype webinar. I'm not going to show you a screenshot of an ad account and tell you that you're one funnel away. You've been sold that before and it cost you real money.
>
> Two things I need from you.
>
> One: be here. I know you're probably between patients. But the money in this hour is worth an hour, and I've watched owners half-watch this and miss the exact number that would've changed their year.
>
> Two: did you bring your numbers? Last month's revenue, what you actually took home, and your lead, consult, and close counts. If you've got them, put a yes in the chat. If you don't, we'll estimate. But if you have them, this stops being a class and becomes an audit of your practice.
>
> And last thing. The replay only goes to people who were here live. That's not a trick, it's a filter. I'd rather have twenty owners who showed up than two hundred who bookmarked it.
>
> Okay. Let's go find your money.

## 5.2 Origin and Permission (0:05 to 0:11)

> Quick on me, and I'll keep it short, because your time is better spent on the frameworks than my resume.
>
> I'm Bethany, co-founder and CEO of The Luxora Collective. We're a revenue growth partner for independent med spas doing roughly five hundred thousand to two million a year.
>
> And I want to tell you why we only work in that range, because it explains everything about how I think.
>
> Under five hundred thousand, everything's a hustle problem, and hustle actually solves it. Over three or four million, you've got infrastructure. A director of operations. A marketing person. A front desk with depth.
>
> But between five hundred thousand and two million? You are the infrastructure. You're the top producer, the closer, the trainer, the marketing department, and the person who fixes it at nine at night. The practice works because you're in it. Which means you're also the ceiling. And it's the loneliest position in this entire industry, because from the outside it looks like success.
>
> Now let me say the thing I actually came here to say.
>
> I've sat across from a lot of owners in this range. And underneath the spreadsheets, it's almost always the same conversation. It usually starts with numbers and about twenty minutes in it turns into something else.
>
> It sounds like: I made more money this year than I've ever made and I'm more scared than I've ever been.
>
> Or: I haven't taken a real vacation in four years.
>
> Or, and this is the one people can barely say out loud: I put my savings into this. Some of you put your house into this. You left a stable career, and everyone told you how brave you were. And the thought that shows up at two in the morning is, what happens if this doesn't work? After everybody believed in me?
>
> If any of that landed, I want you to hear one thing very clearly, and then we'll go to the numbers and I won't be sentimental again for the rest of the hour.
>
> You are not doing this wrong.
>
> You're a clinician who was never handed a business operating system, running a practice that grew faster than its structure, in an industry that only ever sells you more marketing. Of course you're the bottleneck. Nothing was ever built to catch it but you.
>
> That's a structural problem. And structural problems have structural fixes. So let's go.

## 5.3 The Big Domino (0:11 to 0:15)

> Everything in the next forty minutes rests on one idea, so I'm going to spend four minutes on it.
>
> Here it is.
>
> **Revenue that requires you isn't an asset. It's a job with extra risk.**
>
> Let me show you what I mean.
>
> Two practices. Both did a million and a half last year. Identical top line.
>
> Practice A: the owner does sixty percent of the production, closes almost every high-ticket consult personally, and has maybe eleven percent of revenue on any kind of recurring basis. If she's out for two weeks, revenue drops by about half.
>
> Practice B: the owner does twenty percent of production, her team closes at nearly the rate she does because they were trained to, and thirty-five percent of revenue recurs every month before anyone books anything. If she's out for two weeks, revenue moves about four percent.
>
> Same revenue. Completely different businesses.
>
> One of them is worth real money if she ever wants to sell it. One of them is unsellable, because what a buyer would be purchasing is her.
>
> And here's what I need you to sit with. One of those women can take a vacation. And it isn't because she's more disciplined, or works harder, or found some secret. It's because three specific things got built. That's it. Three things.
>
> So when you tell me you want to grow, I'm going to ask you a harder question. Grow which one?
>
> Because if you add three hundred thousand dollars to Practice A, you don't get freedom. You get a heavier version of the exact life that's already wearing you down. More patients, more staff, more decisions, more nights at nine o'clock, and honestly? Not much more money in your pocket, and I'm going to prove that to you in about ninety seconds.
>
> The goal was never more revenue. The goal was revenue that doesn't need you.
>
> Type YES in the chat if you know exactly which practice you're running right now. I want to see it.

## 5.4 Block 1: The Money (0:15 to 0:27)

> Alright. Question one. Where does the money go.
>
> You had a good month. Maybe a great month. And then payroll cleared, and the product invoice hit, and the ad spend went out, and the device lease, and the merchant fees, and you looked at the account and thought: I did everything right. Why does this still feel tight?
>
> Let me explain what's actually happening, because it isn't a mystery and it isn't your spending.
>
> **Number one. Revenue and money are not the same thing.**
>
> A med spa can grow revenue three years straight while the owner takes home less every single year. It happens constantly. It's the most common pattern I see. And the reason is that growth eats cash. Every new patient costs money to acquire before they pay you. Every new hire costs money for months before they produce. Every new device is a payment that starts before the demand does.
>
> So you grow, and the top line goes up, and your life gets harder and your account doesn't change. That's not failure. That's just what unmanaged growth does. But it means the number you've been measuring, revenue, has been lying to you about how you're doing.
>
> **Number two. Here's the number that actually matters, and most owners have never run it.**
>
> Take last month's revenue. Subtract everything. Payroll including yourself, product, rent, marketing, leases, software, fees. What's left, divided by revenue.
>
> That's your operating margin. Write it down right now.
>
> A healthy practice at your size should be in the twenties. A lot of the practices I audit come in single digits, and some come in negative while the owner is telling everyone she had her best year ever.
>
> If you're at eight percent, then every additional hundred thousand of revenue puts eight thousand dollars in your pocket, and costs you significantly more than eight thousand dollars worth of your life.
>
> That's the math behind the exhaustion. That's why the good month doesn't feel good.
>
> **Number three. Now let's find out where it went.** Three places, and it's almost always these three.
>
> **First: your service mix.** You're selling too much of the thing that's busy and not enough of the thing that's profitable. A room hour spent on a low-margin, high-labor service and a room hour spent on a high-margin one look identical on your schedule and completely different on your P&L. Most owners have never run margin by service. When they do, it's the fastest money in the building, because it's a scheduling decision, not a spending decision.
>
> **Second: acquisition cost you can't see.** Take everything you spent last month on getting patients, ads, agency, boosted posts, events, the referral incentive. Divide it by the number of genuinely new patients who paid you. That number is your real cost per patient and it's usually two to four times what the owner guesses.
>
> Now here's the important half. What's a patient worth to you over their entire relationship? Not first purchase. Lifetime. If a patient's worth nine hundred dollars and you're paying four hundred to get her, you have a business problem, not a marketing problem, and no agency change is going to fix that. If she's worth forty-two hundred, you should be spending far more than you are and you're leaving growth on the table because you were scared of a number you never actually calculated.
>
> This is also why the agencies frustrated you. You were evaluating them without the denominator. You could not tell if it was working because you never knew what a patient was worth. So you were guessing, and then arguing about the guess.
>
> **Third: your consult close rate.** Someone took time off work, drove to your building, and sat in front of you. Most practices at your size close forty to fifty percent of those.
>
> Thirty consults a month, twelve hundred average first purchase. At forty-five percent that's sixteen thousand two hundred a month. At sixty-five percent it's twenty-three thousand four hundred. Same consults, same room, same marketing spend.
>
> That's roughly eighty-five thousand dollars a year sitting between two numbers, and it's the highest-margin money in the entire practice because you already paid to get them there.
>
> That's block one. Revenue, margin, mix, acquisition, close rate. Five numbers.
>
> And here's what I want you to notice. Nothing I just described required a single new patient. Every dollar I just pointed at is already inside your building.
>
> In the chat: what's your operating margin? Just the number. I'll react to some of them.

## 5.5 Block 2: The Team (0:27 to 0:36)

> Question two. Why doesn't anybody sell like you do.
>
> I want to start by validating something, and then I'm going to challenge it.
>
> It's true. Nobody in your building sells like you. That's real, I'm not going to tell you it's in your head. Your close rate is higher than theirs. You save the consult they were about to lose. You're the one who can look at a patient and know she needs the treatment plan, not the single syringe.
>
> Now the challenge. That is not a talent gap. And that's why hiring for it keeps failing.
>
> Here's what's actually different about you. Three things.
>
> **You know the outcome the patient is really buying.** She isn't buying units of Botox. She's buying looking like herself again in a photo. You know that and you say it out loud. Your provider says "we'd do about thirty units in the forehead," which is accurate, clinical, and sells nothing.
>
> **You have no fear about the price**, because you know exactly what the result is worth. Your team is quietly embarrassed by your prices. They flinch. And the patient feels the flinch every single time, and reads it as the treatment isn't worth it.
>
> **You always know the next step.** You never end a visit without knowing what happens in six weeks. Your team ends the visit at the visit.
>
> Those three things are teachable. Every one of them. But nobody ever taught them, because in aesthetics we hire clinically and we train clinically and then we act surprised when clinical people behave clinically in a sales conversation.
>
> So here's what has to get installed, and it's two things.
>
> **One: a structured consultation.** Not a script that makes your providers sound like robots. A structure. Same questions asked in the same order every time, the outcome named in the patient's language, the plan presented as a plan rather than an option, and a defined next step before anyone stands up. Then role play until it's boring, and then review real calls and real consults against it.
>
> When we install this, close rates move ten to twenty points, and the fastest movement is almost never from the providers. It's the front desk, because the front desk is currently costing you more money than anyone in the building and nobody's ever measured it.
>
> **Two: compensation that points the same direction as the practice.**
>
> This is the one nobody wants to touch, and it's the actual answer to your staffing problem.
>
> Most med spa comp plans reward showing up. Some reward production in a way that accidentally rewards discounting, or fast turnover of low-value services, or hoarding patients. If your provider makes the same money whether she books the treatment plan or the single syringe, she'll book the single syringe every time, because it's the easier conversation and she's tired too.
>
> When you restructure so that the behavior you need is the behavior that pays them, three things change fast. Performance goes up. Resistance to training drops, because now the training is worth money to them. And retention goes up, which brings me to the expensive part.
>
> **Let's talk about turnover honestly.** You can't find injectors. You can't keep them. The one you finally trained left and took patients with her.
>
> Here's the reframe. A provider who leaves is expensive, but a provider who leaves and takes patients is a symptom of something specific: the patient was loyal to the person instead of to the practice.
>
> That's not a personality issue. It's a design issue. When a patient's relationship lives in a membership, a treatment plan on file, a documented care roadmap, a reputation system, and a front desk that knows her, she belongs to the practice. When it lives in one provider's phone, she belongs to the provider.
>
> You will never fully solve turnover. This industry has a labor shortage and it isn't ending. So stop trying to make people stay and start building a practice where their leaving is survivable. That's the only version of this that actually lets you sleep.
>
> And when you can trust the team, that's when you can leave the building. That's the whole point of this block.

## 5.6 Block 3: The Return (0:36 to 0:44)

> Question three. How do you stop starting every month at zero.
>
> I want to name something first, because I think it's the real source of the anxiety, and it isn't the number.
>
> It's the reset. The first of the month arrives and it's zero and you have to go get it all again. And you've been doing that for years, every thirty days, and it never stops, and no amount of a good month makes the next first of the month feel any different.
>
> That feeling doesn't come from your revenue. It comes from the fact that none of your revenue is committed.
>
> So let's fix the shape of it.
>
> **First: the most expensive thing in your practice right now.**
>
> You spent three hundred dollars to acquire her. She came in, loved it, hugged you at the door, told two friends. And you haven't seen her in fourteen months.
>
> That costs you more than any line item on your P&L, and it appears nowhere on your P&L. It just shows up as a slow month you can't explain.
>
> It costs five to seven times more to acquire a new patient than to bring an existing one back. And most practices your size are sitting on a database of hundreds or thousands of people who purchased, had a great experience, and were never contacted again in any structured way.
>
> That database is the most valuable asset you own and right now it's doing nothing.
>
> **Second: the moment you're losing her.**
>
> It isn't in the treatment room. It's at the front desk, at exit, at the single highest-emotion moment in the entire experience. She's glowing, she loves you, and your front desk says "we'll send you a reminder."
>
> You just handed the most persuadable person in your building over to her own calendar, her own memory, and her own budget four months from now.
>
> Rebooking at exit, required, next appointment scheduled before she leaves the building, costs you nothing and moves retention immediately. It's a policy change. That's all it is.
>
> **Third: build revenue that exists before the month starts.**
>
> A properly built membership changes the shape of the business.
>
> And I want to be specific, because most med spa memberships are quietly destroying margin. A discount club is not a membership. If your membership is "ten percent off everything," you've built a program that reduces revenue from your best patients, who were going to come anyway.
>
> A real membership is built on the treatment cadence you actually want the patient on, priced against lifetime value instead of against your competitor down the street, with retail attached, and with a benefit structure that makes leaving feel like a loss.
>
> When thirty percent of your revenue is committed before the first of the month, everything changes. You can forecast. You can hire before you're desperate. You can negotiate with vendors from a position of strength. You can look at a slow week without your stomach dropping.
>
> That's what predictable actually means. Not bigger. Predictable.
>
> **And here's where the three blocks come together.**
>
> Fix your margin and mix, and the money stops disappearing.
>
> Train and align the team, and revenue stops depending on you personally.
>
> Build retention and recurring revenue, and the month stops starting at zero.
>
> Do all three and you have Practice B. You have something that's worth money, that survives a resignation, that lets you take a week off, and that you could sell someday if you wanted to.
>
> That's freedom. And notice that not one thing I described was a new ad campaign.

## 5.7 The Bridge (0:44 to 0:46)

> So that's the framework. It's real, it's yours, and if you execute it alone over the next year you'll be better off for this hour.
>
> And I want to be honest about what usually happens, because I've watched it enough times.
>
> Most of you are going to feel clear for about seventy-two hours. Then Monday happens. A provider calls out. The schedule blows up. Somebody leaves a bad review. And by Thursday this hour is one more thing you meant to get to.
>
> That's not a discipline problem. Look at what I just asked you to do. Rebuild your comp plan. Restructure your service mix. Design and launch a membership. Train your entire team on a consultation structure. Build a reactivation system. Install rebooking protocols.
>
> That's a full-time job. And I'm asking the person who's already the top producer, the closer, and the safety net to also do it. Alone. While making forty other decisions a week about lasers and vendors and hiring with nobody to check her thinking against.
>
> That's the actual reason it doesn't get done. Not knowledge. Capacity.
>
> So for the people here who don't want this to be another good Tuesday that changed nothing, let me tell you exactly what we do and how it works. Ten minutes. If it's not for you, stay anyway, because I'm doing Q&A and I'll answer anything about your own numbers.

## 5.8 THE OFFER (0:46 to 0:57)

An agency is four to eight thousand a month and doesn't touch operations. Then compare it to the leaks. >
> If you know, apply for the Blueprint Call. Three spots.
>
> If you're not there, take the twenty-nine dollar audit. Everyone should do that one.
>

Cut the highest-converting recording into an evergreen replay funnel and run cold traffic continuously. Keep one live event monthly for fresh material and testimonials. Live is where the offer gets sharpened. Evergreen is where it scales.
